project_title: Mini RDBMS Engine with Query Processing & Transaction Support
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Mini RDBMS Engine with Query Processing & Transaction Support
problem_statement: In real-world applications, databases handle data creation, queries, modifications and security, but internal processes such as query processing, optimization, concurrency control and crash recovery often remain a black box to students. The proposed Mini RDBMS Engine with Query Processing & Transaction Support aims to demonstrate these processes by implementing a SQL-like query processor, semantic validation, indexing, query execution and transaction management with commit, rollback and simulated crash recovery.
objectives:
To implement a lexer, parser and semantic checker that convert SQL text into a validated parse tree and reject invalid queries with clear, position-aware error messages.
To design a storage engine that supports DML commands on the stored tables.
To build a query-execution engine that chooses an choosing algorithm for each query and returns correct results.
To implement transaction management with BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK, backed by an undo log, so that a failed or interrupted transaction leaves zero partial changes.
To demonstrate, through a command-line interface, how a single SQL statement moves from parsing through optimization and execution to a transactionally safe result.
technologies: Design & Analysis of Algorithms (DAA): Time-complexity (Big-O) analysis, searching, hashing and indexing structures used to compare and choose a query's access path  Hash indexing, B-Tree range indexing, binary search, Big-O comparison of scan vs index-lookup cost; Operating System Principles: Process/thread synchronization, locking (mutex/semaphore) for concurrent sessions, deadlock avoidance, file I/O, buffering, and crash recovery; Principles of Compiler Design (POCD): Lexical analysis, grammar (CFG), recursive-descent parsing, syntax-tree (AST) construction, and semantic analysis of SQL statements; Database Management Systems: Relational model, tables/tuples/attributes, primary/foreign keys and constraints, ACID properties, catalog management and normalization

project_title: Multi-Process Search Engine with Persistent Index
abstract: Figure: Conceptual Workflow and System Architecture — PaperLens Multi-Process Search Engine
problem_statement:
In today's digital world, large volumes of information are generated and stored in documents, files, and databases. Retrieving relevant information efficiently from this growing data is a major challenge. Traditional search systems often perform indexing and searching sequentially within a single process. As the volume of data increases, this approach can lead to higher execution time, inefficient resource utilization, and slower query responses.

A Multi-Process Search Engine with Persistent Indexing aims to overcome these limitations by using multiple independent processes to perform indexing and searching concurrently.

Our project, PaperLens, applies this idea to computer-science research papers: parallel reader processes prepare papers and citations, a persistent index stays consistent even after a crash, and search combines keyword, semantic and citation signals.
objectives:
1. Build a multi-process pipeline that collects paper records and citations and prepares them in parallel.
2. Design a persistent on-disk index that survives crashes and restarts without being left half-written.
3. Use process synchronization and logging so several reader processes and one writer update the index safely.
4. Create a search component that combines keyword, semantic and citation signals to return top-k results.
5. Set up a process manager that recovers worker crashes automatically, and evaluate search quality.
technologies: Operating Systems: Multi-process design, inter-process communication (shared memory, queues), synchronization, process supervision and restart, file durability (fsync); Database Management Systems: Write-ahead logging, atomic commit, crash recovery, on-disk index organisation, consistent reads during writes, compaction; Data Structures and Algorithms: Inverted index, tokenization, BM25 ranking, heaps for top-k retrieval, hashing (Bloom filter, MinHash), graph ranking (PageRank); Computer Networks: HTTP communication with arXiv and OpenAlex, request rate limiting and retries, politeness towards public services; Discrete Mathematics: Graph theory (citation graph), set similarity (near-duplicate detection), probability behind hashing and ranking; Software Engineering: Modular multi-engine design, sprint-based delivery, requirement traceability, integration and crash testing

project_title: Large-Scale Log Processing & Analytics Engine
abstract: Fig 1. Single-Machine Log Processing Pipeline Conceptual Workflow
problem_statement:
Modern applications and servers generate log files that grow to many gigabytes. Each line is unstructured text, and the files often contain malformed lines and repeated entries. Because of this, the logs cannot be searched or analysed directly, and loading such a file fully into memory is not practical on an ordinary machine.

This project builds a single-machine pipeline that reads one massive log file efficiently, converts raw lines into structured records, removes bad and duplicate data, stores the clean records in a database and presents analytics on a web dashboard.
objectives:
Read a very large single log file in newline-aligned chunks using memory mapping, without loading the whole file into RAM.
Parse each raw line into structured fields (timestamp, level, IP address, error code, message) and validate them, sending malformed lines to a quarantine store with a reason.
Remove duplicate records with a bounded sliding-window fingerprint set so that memory use stays flat.
Store clean records in PostgreSQL through in-memory micro-batches and bulk inserts, with retry on failed writes.
Provide aggregate analytics (counts by level, error code and time) through a REST API with time-range and log-level filters, shown on a live web dashboard.
technologies: Operating Systems: Memory-mapped files (mmap), virtual memory and page cache, file descriptors, system calls, chunked I/O; Data Structures & Algorithms: Regular-expression parsing, hashing and fingerprints, hash sets, queues, sliding-window eviction, complexity analysis; Database Management Systems: Relational schema design, bulk insert, transactions, indexing, aggregate SQL, query tuning; Web Technologies: REST API design, HTTP and JSON, client-side charts, filtering through query parameters

project_title: Large-Scale Dataset Profiling & Data Quality Engine
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Large-Scale Dataset Profiling & Data Quality Engine
problem_statement: Structured datasets can contain missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent types, invalid values, and statistically unusual observations. The proposed project brings dataset profiling and data-quality assessment into a single workflow so users can inspect a dataset, identify quality issues, select supported corrections, and revalidate the results. The presentations describe an upload-to-report workflow and emphasize preserving the original dataset while applying corrections to a separate copy.

To accept supported structured/tabular datasets and generate a structural profile.
To identify missing values, duplicate rows, data-type inconsistencies, and rule violations.
To compute descriptive statistics and flag potentially unusual observations.
To allow users to review detected issues and apply selected supported corrections without changing the original dataset.
To revalidate corrected data and present data-quality results and reports.

project_title: Mini-kernel with process, memory and file management
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Mini-kernel with process, memory and file management
problem_statement:
Our project focuses on understanding how a computer can start and run its own basic operating-system kernel. A kernel is the core part of an operating system that manages access to hardware resources and provides essential services to programs. Developing even a small kernel involves several connected responsibilities, such as starting execution after boot, managing memory, handling processes, and organizing data on storage.

Our proposed mini-kernel is a small x86-64 operating-system kernel developed from the ground up for learning and demonstration. It will be loaded by a bootloader and executed in an emulated computer environment during development. The project aims to implement selected kernel-level facilities and demonstrate how they work together. The work will use xv6 and other educational resources only for understanding operating-system concepts; the xv6 codebase will not be used as the project foundation.

We consider this a suitable Mini Project because it gives us an opportunity to study operating-system fundamentals through implementation rather than only theoretical discussion. A controlled scope will allow us to demonstrate the basic working of a kernel without attempting to build a complete commercial operating system.
objectives:
To understand the role of a kernel in an operating system and study the basic stages involved in starting kernel execution.
To design and develop a small x86-64 kernel from scratch, using an existing bootloader as the initial loading mechanism.
To explore and implement selected fundamental kernel responsibilities related to process, memory and file management.
To demonstrate the kernel in an emulated hardware environment and observe its behaviour during execution.
To apply foundational Computer Science and system-software concepts through a practical, demonstrable operating-system project.
technologies: Operating System Principles: Kernel responsibilities, process management, memory management, file systems, interrupts and resource management; Computer Organization and Architecture: Processor basics, boot process, CPU operation, memory hierarchy and hardware interaction; Data Structures & Algorithms: Queues, lists, trees or other suitable structures, searching, scheduling concepts and efficient management of kernel data

project_title: Java Compiler and Bytecode Generation Engine
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Java Compiler and Bytecode Generation Engine
problem_statement:
Java source programs pass through several compilation stages before they can be executed by the Java Virtual Machine. These stages include lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic checking, intermediate representation generation, code optimization and bytecode generation. Studying these stages separately can make it difficult to understand how they work together in a complete compiler.

The implemented project is a Java Compiler and Bytecode Generation Engine for a defined Java subset. It uses a Flex-based lexer and a Bison parser based on a 53-rule grammar to process source programs and construct an Abstract Syntax Tree. The compiler performs semantic analysis using scoped symbol information, generates Three-Address Code (TAC), applies intermediate-code optimization passes, and uses a Java ASM backend to generate JVM class files. The C++ front end exports the optimized, type-annotated program as a typed intermediate representation (JSON), which the Java ASM backend reads to produce the class file. The generated class is then executed on the JVM, so the complete flow is organised as seven phases: scanner, parser, semantic analysis, TAC generation, optimization, bytecode generation and execution.

The project also provides a web-based interface for demonstrating the compilation phases and viewing their intermediate results, optimization information, generated bytecode and execution output. The implementation is limited to the language constructs supported by its grammar and backend; it is not a complete Java compiler.
objectives:
To develop an integrated compiler pipeline that processes programs written using the supported Java language subset.
To implement lexical analysis, grammar-based syntax analysis, AST construction and semantic checking.
To generate Three-Address Code and apply intermediate-representation optimization techniques.
To generate JVM bytecode using the Java ASM backend, execute the generated class using the existing JVM and inspect the program output.
To provide a web-based demonstration interface through which users can inspect the major compilation phases and their results.
technologies: Principles of Compiler Design: Regular expressions and lexical patterns; tokens; Context-Free Grammar (CFG); BNF productions; Flex-based lexical analysis; Bison LALR(1) parsing; syntax-directed AST construction; semantic analysis; intermediate-code and bytecode generation.; Data Structures and Algorithms: Abstract Syntax Trees and tree traversal; scoped symbol tables and hash-based lookup; stacks for parser/scope processing; vectors and maps for tokens and IR; Three-Address Code; control-flow labels; optimization passes including constant folding, constant propagation, copy propagation, common subexpression elimination and dead-code/branch elimination.; Object-Oriented Programming: C++ classes and objects; structures and enumerations; inheritance and polymorphism where used in AST/compiler components; modular design and encapsulation.; Java, JVM and Web Technology: Java-based ASM backend; JVM class files, bytecode, operand stack and local variables; HTML, CSS and JavaScript interface; Python standard-library web server for displaying compilation phases and results.

project_title: Incremental Build & Dependency Resolution Tool
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Incremental Build and Dependency Resolution Tool
problem_statement:
Software projects often contain multiple build actions that depend on one another. When a source file changes, running every build action again can repeat work that is not required. Developers need a reliable way to identify the affected actions, respect dependency order and reuse previously generated outputs only when those outputs are still valid.

The proposed Incremental Build and Dependency Resolution Tool addresses this problem through file fingerprinting, dependency-graph analysis, build planning, task execution and artifact caching. The extended prototype also explores controlled execution of suitable independent actions on trusted computers connected through a local-area network (LAN).
objectives:
To create a project manifest describing build actions, commands, inputs, outputs and dependencies.
To detect added, modified, deleted and unchanged files using SHA-256 fingerprints, and identify the build actions affected by those changes.
To represent build actions as a directed dependency graph, detect dependency cycles and determine a valid execution order.
To schedule and execute eligible actions as operating-system processes with bounded local parallelism, and investigate controlled TCP-based execution on trusted LAN workers.
To reuse cached artifacts only when the complete declared action identity and expected outputs are valid, while persistently maintaining file state, artifact metadata and build history.
To evaluate correctness and performance by comparing clean builds, incremental builds, cache reuse, and local versus networked execution.
technologies: Data Structures and Algorithms / Design and Analysis of Algorithms: Directed graphs, adjacency lists, hash maps/sets, BFS/DFS, topological sorting and cycle detection; Operating Systems: File and process operations, process exit codes, worker pools, synchronization, concurrency limits and task-state management; Database Management Systems: SQLite tables, keys, CRUD operations, transactions, build history and persistent metadata; Computer Networks: TCP client-server communication, message framing, worker registration, heartbeats, timeouts, task dispatch and artifact transfer; Object-Oriented Programming: Interfaces and classes for adapters, actions, scheduler, cache, state repository, coordinator and workers

project_title: Resilient Multi-Peer File Distribution & Recovery Engine
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Resilient Multi-Peer File Distribution & Recovery Engine
problem_statement:
In a multi-peer file distribution environment, a file may be divided into smaller portions and distributed among multiple participating peers for storage and transfer. Successful retrieval of the complete file therefore depends on the availability and accessibility of the required portions across the participating peers.

In practical distributed environments, peers may become temporarily unavailable due to process termination, network interruption or other failures. Such unavailability can make required file portions inaccessible and may interrupt file retrieval or prevent successful reconstruction. Repeatedly depending on the same unavailable peer can further increase recovery time and communication overhead.

The proposed Resilient Multi-Peer File Distribution & Recovery Engine aims to study and develop a system that can continue file distribution and retrieval despite defined peer failures. The project focuses on identifying unavailable data, obtaining the required information from available participating peers, verifying recovered data and reconstructing the original file.
objectives:
To develop a multi-peer file distribution system capable of dividing and distributing file data among participating peers.
To enable the system to identify unavailable or failed peers and determine the impact on ongoing file retrieval.
To provide a recovery mechanism that can retrieve missing file data from available surviving replicas on participating peers and reconstruct the original file.
To verify recovered data and successfully reconstruct the requested file after supported peer failures.
To study the behaviour of the system under different controlled peer availability and failure conditions.
technologies: Design & Analysis of Algorithms (DAA): Chunking, distribution strategy, replica/source selection, searching, ordering and reconstruction.; Computer Networks: Peer communication, data transfer, addressing, connection management and network failures.; Operating Systems: Processes, process lifecycle, file handling, resource management and process failure.; Distributed Systems: Peer-based resource sharing, replication, fault tolerance, availability and failure handling.; Database Management Systems (DBMS): Metadata storage, chunk-to-peer mapping, peer status and efficient metadata lookup.; Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): Modular system design using components such as Peer, Chunk, Transfer and Recovery.

project_title: Network Traffic Monitoring & Protocol Analysis Tool
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Mini-Shark Network Traffic Monitoring & Protocol Analysis Tool
problem_statement:
Network administrators use packet-capture utilities, connectivity tests and interface statistics to understand network behaviour. However, a packet capture taken at only one location gives limited visibility into what happens along the complete network path. An observation at the sending point cannot by itself show whether the same traffic was delayed, changed or failed to appear at a later observation point. Synthetic tests such as ICMP ping may also not represent the behaviour of real application traffic. In addition, heavy traffic can make monitoring itself more difficult because capture and processing may not keep up with incoming packets.

Mini-Shark is proposed as a network traffic monitoring and protocol analysis tool that observes live traffic at more than one point in a controlled network, compares the observations and presents useful diagnostic information. It aims to help an operator investigate transit delay and unmatched observations while making clear that a missing observation may also result from capture or telemetry limitations, rather than automatically proving network-path loss. The proposed work will be demonstrated in a controlled virtual laboratory.
objectives:
To study how network traffic can be observed at multiple points along a communication path.
To develop a tool that captures and analyses selected live network traffic for monitoring purposes.
To compare packet observations from different points and estimate transit delay where timestamps are comparable.
To identify unmatched observations for further investigation without treating them automatically as confirmed network loss.
To evaluate the monitoring tool under normal, concurrent, delayed and high-traffic test conditions.
technologies: Computer Networks: Network communication, Ethernet and IP addressing, TCP/UDP, routing, packet behaviour and network performance.; Operating System Principles: Network interfaces, packet capture, processes and threads, producer-consumer concepts, buffering and resource management.; Data Structures & Algorithms: Efficient organization and comparison of packet observations, searching, matching and time-based processing concepts.; Database Management Systems: Organizing, storing and retrieving probe observations, monitoring events and diagnostic summaries.

project_title: HTTP Proxy Server with In-Memory Caching
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of HTTP Proxy Server with In-Memory Caching
problem_statement:
When several users on the same network access the same web resource, each request may travel to the origin server even when the resource has not changed. This repeated communication increases response time and uses network bandwidth unnecessarily. In places such as college labs, hostels and shared networks, many users may request the same pages or static resources.

Our proposed HTTP Proxy Server with In-Memory Caching is intended to reduce this repetition by placing a proxy between the client and the origin server. The proxy receives a request and checks whether a suitable, fresh response is already available in its memory. If it is available, the response can be returned to the client without contacting the origin server again. If it is not available or is no longer fresh, the proxy contacts the origin server and forwards the response to the client.
objectives:
To study how repeated requests for unchanged web resources affect response time and network bandwidth.
To develop an HTTP proxy that accepts client requests and communicates with the required origin server.
To reuse suitable cached responses for repeated requests while ensuring that only fresh responses are served.
To reduce unnecessary communication with origin servers and study the effect of caching on response time and bandwidth usage.
To apply Computer Networks, algorithm design and Operating Systems concepts in a practical networking system and evaluate its behaviour under multiple client requests.
technologies: Computer Networks: Client-server communication, TCP sockets, ports, HTTP request-response flow and proxy communication.; Design & Analysis of Algorithms (DAA): Efficient searching, average-case lookup, cache replacement decisions and time/space complexity.; Operating System Principles: Processes and threads, concurrent request handling, synchronization, shared resources and resource management.; Software Engineering: Requirement analysis, modular development, testing, benchmarking, documentation and version control.

project_title: Constraint-Based Academic Timetable Scheduling
abstract: Fig 1. Conceptual Workflow of Constraint-Based Academic Timetable Scheduling
problem_statement:
Preparing an academic timetable involves coordinating courses, sections, faculty members, classrooms, laboratories and time slots while satisfying multiple interdependent constraints. Factors such as faculty and room availability, prescribed weekly teaching hours, fixed breaks and consecutive laboratory sessions make the scheduling process particularly complex.

Manual or iterative scheduling often requires repeated conflict checks, as resolving one conflict may introduce another. A faculty member may be assigned to overlapping classes, a section may receive two courses in the same time slot, or a room may be allocated to more than one class simultaneously. These conflicts can require repeated timetable revisions and make it difficult to maintain consistent schedules for all stakeholders.

The proposed Constraint-Based Academic Timetable Scheduling Engine aims to develop a structured system that models academic entities and scheduling rules, generates timetables that satisfy mandatory constraints, considers preferential requirements where feasible, and reports diagnostic information when no feasible schedule can be produced. The primary stakeholders are the Timetable Coordinator, Department Head (HoD), faculty members, and students/sections. Secondary stakeholders include room and laboratory coordinators and academic administration.
objectives:
To develop a structured data model for courses, sections, faculty members, classrooms, laboratories and scheduling time slots.
To identify, classify and represent mandatory (hard) and preferential (soft) scheduling constraints.
To generate academic timetables that satisfy all mandatory constraints and eliminate resource-allocation conflicts.
To incorporate faculty availability and workload considerations into the scheduling process.
To provide consistent and synchronized timetable views for classes, faculty members and rooms.
To generate meaningful conflict information and diagnostic feedback when no feasible timetable can be produced.
technologies: Data Structures and Algorithms: Backtracking, search strategies, conflict detection and optimization techniques.; Database Management Systems (DBMS): Relational data modelling, SQL, CRUD operations, transaction management and scheduling records.; Discrete Mathematics: Sets, relations, propositional logic, combinatorial modelling and constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs).; Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): Classes, objects, encapsulation, abstraction and modular software design.; Operating Systems: Scheduling principles, resource allocation and resource-conflict management.; Software Engineering: Requirements analysis, UML modelling, feasibility assessment and software testing.

project_title: Smart Campus Lab and Resource Optimizer
abstract: Conceptual Flow - Smart Campus Lab & Resource Optimizer
problem_statement: In many colleges, academic timetables and resource allocation are still managed manually, making it difficult to handle sudden changes, additional classes, and faculty unavailability. These challenges often result in scheduling conflicts, underutilized classrooms and laboratories, and uneven faculty workloads. Managing multiple scheduling requests is also complicated due to the lack of a systematic approach to prioritizing requests, ensuring fairness, and considering resource availability. Therefore, an efficient system is needed to simplify timetable management, optimize the use of existing resources, and ensure smooth academic activities with minimal disruption.
objectives:
To detect overlapping booking requests and resource conflicts accurately.
To allocate resources while following capacity, time-slot and eligibility rules.
To improve resource utilization and fairness compared with first-come-first-served allocation.
To identify and report requests that cannot be fulfilled when resources are limited.
To generate reports on resource utilization, fairness and conflicts.
To test the system with increasing numbers of booking requests.
